extracted.intended_audience: college instructors designing or teaching guided-discovery discrete math and geometry courses for pre-service middle-school (and elementary) mathematics teachers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and assessing a guided-discovery discrete mathematics course (and related middle-grades geometry course) for pre-service middle-school teachers, including homework, exams, projects, participation, and class format expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework sets (frequency and purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary homework assignments (exercises) modeled on the problem sequences from the notes were assigned about every 3–4 weeks to allow students to accumulate familiarity with a topic before applying it to homework exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish 'problems' (numbered questions in the notes) from 'exercises' (questions on supplemental homework). Homework sets provide the principal opportunity for individual demonstration of mastery and for individual feedback and evaluation from the instructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homework solutions: explanation and notation expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Students were expected to explain their solutions carefully from beginning to end with clearly written justifications; rigorous formalism was not required but detailed and logical explanations and proper notation and terminology were expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructor provided substantial feedback on written work; homework sets were the main mechanism to improve students' written communication. Anti-pattern: writing just enough so the instructor can 'fill in' omitted details. Example improvement: move from minimal notes to clear narrative with supporting examples and contextual notation (e.g., c1,... and f1,... instead of raw numerals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exam format and expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Two in-class exams (a midterm and a comprehensive final) containing computational and short-answer explanation questions that require students to apply what they have studied to new situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exams assess individual mastery similarly to homework; review days are used to prepare students to take stock of accumulated knowledge before the midterm and final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review-day preparatory activities
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparatory work for review days consists of listing and defining key principles and terms (both formally and in students' own words), illustrating these with examples, identifying problems in the notes that exemplify different concepts, creating one's own problems that use the same techniques, and determining lingering confusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review periods begin with small-group discussion (peer answers many questions) and conclude with the instructor addressing remaining concerns on the board. This activity is intended to help students 'take stock' of accumulated knowledge and reveal areas needing clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional module project requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Final project: develop an instructional module at the level of the students' home classroom on a discrete-math topic not explicitly covered in the course. Each project has a written component and a 15-minute oral presentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written component should include explanation of mathematical content, lesson plans, worksheets, and general guidance for a teacher. Students are encouraged (but not required) to incorporate hands-on investigations and experimental classroom activities. Students may work individually or in pairs (instructor preferred pairs to simplify scheduling and encourage collaboration). Two groups piloted activities in a partner's classroom prior to class presentation. Assessment specifics referenced to the project instruction sheet (assessment rubric on last page of instructions). Project weight in grade = 15%.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading scheme and assessment policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Most assessment for the course is based on individual work. Course grade percentages were allocated as: overall participation 10%; written solutions to homework sets 35%; instructional module project 15%; in-class midterm exam 20%; in-class final exam 20%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on individual demonstration of mastery despite heavy use of group discussion during class. The instructor provided clear assessments so students could be reassured about grading in a nontraditional format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation evaluation rubric (0–5 scale)
rubrics_metrics.description: Overall participation grades were based on preparation of assigned problems, quality of involvement in small groups, contributions to whole-class discussions, and presentations of solutions. The instructor assessed participation weekly and assigned each student a score out of 5 possible points, using a rubric distinguishing levels 0–5 provided at the start of term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most students earned full five points; early in the semester some students received four due to reluctance to talk in groups. Weekly scoring, rubric provided up front, and instructor feedback helped students improve to full participation over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-class behavior and presentation norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical class meetings are centered on small-group problem solving with volunteers presenting solutions at the board; class discussion and sharing of strategies are integral. Students are expected to engage in dynamic mathematical discussions, present work publicly, and listen carefully to peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instructors should reassure students that group discussion is integral (not remedial), encourage generalizations beyond the problem statement, accept unpolished ideas, and frame mistakes as part of learning. If a presenting group does not know an answer, that is acceptable and can lead to rich discussion. The instructor's role is to ask guiding questions and exemplify strategies like checking small cases and searching for counterexamples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of concrete contexts to introduce abstract concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce abstract mathematics through concrete contexts, models, and examples, minimizing technical jargon so topics are conducive to experimentation and intuitive discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: functions via candy-distribution to emphasize domain/codomain choices and injectivity/surjectivity; recursion via Cuisenaire rod arrangements to motivate and justify recursive formulas (Fibonacci); Ramsey numbers introduced through acquaintances/strangers stories before formal graph abstractions. Pedagogical advantage: helps students connect intuition to formal notions and supports investigative learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course learning objectives (Geometry for Middle Grades Teachers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should be able to problem-solve in geometry; use dynamic software to aid problem solving; use mathematical modeling to solve geometric problems; make conjectures based on observations; present clear and concise explanations; and reason mathematically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These objectives are met through exploration and investigation of geometric ideas (topology, shapes in plane and space, motions, similarity and measurement). Assessment and activities (hands-on, constructions, manipulatives, technology, presentations) should align to these objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical class meeting structure and logistics
rubrics_metrics.description: A class meeting begins with a brief introduction or motivating question, then students work in small groups (often on different problems), followed by group presentations and class Q&A. If presentations run over, they continue in the next class and process repeats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are required to print and bring course notes/handouts to each meeting. Instructor facilitates but student active participation and presentations are essential. The process emphasizes cooperative problem solving and multiple representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topology teaching criterion (conceptual approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach topological equivalence by focusing on allowed deformations: 'stretching,' 'squeezing,' and 'twisting' without tearing; use classic concrete examples (coffee mug vs. donut) and guided questions (e.g., which letters of the alphabet are topologically equivalent?).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples and instructor-led discussion to contrast equivalence vs. topological equivalence and to provoke student intuition and dialogue.
